justification_text:
My point estimates were anchored primarily to the prevailing price level of the asset at the time of forecasting, with modest drift built in at each horizon. For the 1-day estimate, I assumed mean-reverting behavior around the recent trading range, expecting little directional movement absent a clear catalyst, which placed the estimate near the last observed price. At the 1-week horizon, I allowed for a slightly higher estimate reflecting a mild upward drift assumption consistent with longer-run momentum, while acknowledging that a week provides enough time for meaningful price discovery. At the 1-month horizon, I incorporated a somewhat larger upward drift, reflecting the idea that over a month, broader macro tailwinds or fundamental revaluation tendencies tend to nudge prices modestly higher on average, though the effect is small relative to the uncertainty introduced at that timeframe.

The confidence interval widths were driven by the standard scaling of uncertainty with time. At 1 day, daily volatility is relatively contained, so the 90% interval was fairly narrow — roughly plus or minus 15 points around the point estimate. By 1 week, volatility compounds, and I widened the interval considerably to account for the possibility of multi-day trending moves or reversals. At 1 month, the interval nearly triples in width, reflecting that a month is long enough for significant macro developments, earnings surprises, policy shifts, or sentiment regime changes to materialize. I also factored in that realized volatility can cluster — quiet periods can be interrupted by sudden spikes — which adds fat-tail risk beyond what simple Gaussian scaling would suggest.

Several specific risks could push outcomes outside my stated intervals. On the downside, a sudden deterioration in risk sentiment — triggered by geopolitical escalation, a surprise central bank policy shift, or a significant macro data disappointment — could cause sharp selling that breaches the lower bound, particularly at the 1-week and 1-month horizons. On the upside, an unexpectedly strong economic release, a dovish pivot signal, or a short-squeeze dynamic could push prices well above the upper bound. Liquidity conditions also matter; in thinner markets, moves can overshoot fair value substantially. These tail events, while individually unlikely, collectively represent a meaningful probability of outcomes outside the stated 90% intervals, which by construction are already expected to be violated roughly 10% of the time even under normal conditions.
